source.title: Custom Tablecloth Styles: Throw, Fitted, Stretch, and Runner Covers
source.body:
A table is more than a place to put brochures or products. At a trade show, market, conference, or corporate event, it is part of the first impression. A branded cloth can make the station easier to recognize, hide visual clutter, and connect the tabletop to the rest of the display. The right style depends on how the table will be used, how much of it needs to be covered, and whether you prefer a relaxed drape or a close, tailored fit. The broader[ SignageBuzz Canada event-display collection](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/) can help you think about the table as one part of the complete setup.
This guide compares four common custom tablecloth styles: the traditional throw, the fitted cover, the stretch cover, and the table runner. The[ SignageBuzz custom tablecloth collection](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/custom-tablecloths) describes these formats for branded event setups, with rectangular table options commonly organized around 4-foot, 6-foot, and 8-foot tables. Use the comparison below as a planning guide, then confirm the exact measurements and configuration for the product you select.
What Are the Main Custom Tablecloth Styles?
The four styles serve different visual and practical purposes:
•Throw cover: A loose cloth that drapes over the table and creates a classic event look.
•Fitted cover: A tailored cover shaped to the table, with a neater, more structured silhouette.
•Stretch cover: A tensioned fabric cover that pulls close to the tabletop and legs for a sleek appearance.
•Runner cover: A branded strip placed over a plain tablecloth or venue-provided table covering.
Some suppliers use “tablecloth,” “table cover,” and “table throw” interchangeably. The important distinction is how the fabric sits on the table. A throw leaves more room for variation, while fitted and stretch formats require closer attention to the table’s actual dimensions. A runner provides a branding layer without replacing the base cover.
1. Throw Tablecloths: The Traditional, Flexible Option
A throw, also called a standard or loose table cover, drapes over the tabletop and down the sides. It is the familiar choice for trade-show tables, registration desks, school events, vendor booths, and corporate presentations. The[ standard table cover range](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/standard-table-covers) lists 4-foot, 6-foot, and 8-foot rectangular formats, with three-sided and four-sided coverage options.
Why choose a throw?
The main advantage is flexibility. A loose cover can accommodate small differences between tables that are nominally the same size. That can matter when an event organizer supplies the furniture or when a team uses tables from more than one venue. The soft drape also creates a conventional, approachable look that suits many brands.
A three-sided throw keeps the back open. Staff can sit behind the table and reach stored materials more easily. A four-sided throw covers the back as well, producing a more complete branded appearance and helping conceal boxes or spare supplies.
What to watch for
A throw can bunch at the corners or move more easily than a fitted style. Smooth the front before visitors arrive, and keep the hem away from walkways. If wind is a concern, ask the supplier which construction is appropriate and secure the table and display according to venue rules. A tablecloth should not be treated as an anchoring system.
2. Fitted Tablecloths: A Clean, Tailored Silhouette
A fitted cover is cut and sewn to follow the shape of a particular table. Instead of hanging loosely, it creates a closer profile with defined corners. The[ fitted table cover page](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/custom-tablecloths/fitted-table-covers) lists three-sided, four-sided, and four-sided-with-zipper configurations for rectangular tables in several sizes.
Why choose a fitted cover?
Fitted covers are a strong choice when a polished, architectural appearance matters. The closer fit keeps the front and sides visually controlled, which is useful when the table will be photographed or viewed from multiple directions. Full coverage can also keep stored items out of sight, while a three-sided version preserves rear access.
A zippered configuration can provide a practical access point without leaving the entire back open. Consider how staff will retrieve literature, samples, or personal items before choosing the configuration.
What to watch for
A fitted cover is less forgiving of measurement errors than a loose throw. Confirm the table length, depth, height, corner shape, and any unusual legs or frame parts. A venue’s “6-foot table” may not match the dimensions of a table owned by your organization. If you are buying a complete table-and-cover solution, a[ folding table with fitted table cover](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/folding-table-with-fitted-table-cover) can simplify the matching process.
3. Stretch Tablecloths: A Sleek, Tensioned Look
A stretch cover uses elastic fabric to create a taut silhouette around the table. Rather than relying on a loose drop, the material is pulled into place so the front and sides look smooth and close to the structure. This style suits brands that want a contemporary, streamlined presentation.
The[ stretch table cover page](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/custom-tablecloths/stretch-table-covers) is the relevant product destination for this format. Because stretch covers depend on tension, accurate table measurements are especially important. Check the table’s length, depth, height, leg position, and base shape before ordering.
Why choose a stretch cover?
A stretch cover can reduce visible loose fabric and create a strong modern outline. It works well for technology demonstrations, premium product displays, contemporary conferences, and booths where a crisp visual system matters. It can also be useful when the table will be seen from the sides and the brand wants consistent coverage around the structure.
What to watch for
Do not assume that a stretch cover will fit every table labelled with the same nominal size. Fixed feet, unusual legs, thick tabletops, or a different table depth can affect the result. Allow enough time for a careful proof and fit check, especially when the table is supplied by the venue.
4. Table Runners: Focused Branding with Less Coverage
A runner is a long branded strip placed over the centre of a table. It can sit on a plain tablecloth, a neutral solid-color base, or a venue-provided cover. The[ custom table runner page](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/table-runner) describes 300D polyester runners with full-colour dye-sublimation printing and rectangular table formats.
Why choose a runner?
A runner is useful when you want a visible logo or message without replacing the entire table covering. It is also practical for organizations that already own neutral tablecloths or need to update campaigns more often than they replace their base covers. Different runners can support different events while the underlying cloth remains consistent.
A runner can create a lighter visual treatment, leaving space for brochures, samples, or products on either side. It is also easier to coordinate with a table that does not match a standard trade-show size, although you should still check the length, width, and desired overhang.
What to watch for
Do not place the primary message where products will cover it. Decide whether the runner should hang over the front and back, over the ends, or finish near the tabletop edge. The source category guidance describes runners as commonly 24 to 36 inches wide, with a 6- to 12-inch overhang often used for a traditional setup; treat those figures as planning guidance and confirm the actual product dimensions before ordering.
Throw vs. Fitted vs. Stretch vs. Runner: A Quick Comparison
A throw is usually the most forgiving option when table dimensions may vary. A fitted cover is better when you want a tailored shape and can confirm the measurements. A stretch cover emphasizes a tight, contemporary silhouette and needs careful fit planning. A runner is the lightest branding option and works best when the table already has a suitable base.
Think of the decision as a balance between coverage, fit, access, and visual style. A four-sided throw or fitted cover gives more complete concealment. A three-sided version makes rear access easier. A stretch cover prioritizes a close appearance. A runner prioritizes flexibility and a smaller branding footprint.
How to Choose the Right Style
Start with the table, not the artwork
Measure the actual table you will use. Record its length, depth, height, tabletop thickness, corner profile, and leg placement. If the table comes from a venue, request the specifications before designing the artwork. A fitted or stretch cover should not be ordered from a rough estimate.
If you are working in a compact booth, compare the table with the rest of the display. A[ 10-foot trade-show display](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/trade-show-displays/10ft-displays) may provide a larger visual backdrop, while the tablecloth handles lower-level branding and storage concealment.
Decide how much access you need
Choose three-sided coverage when staff need easy access behind the table or when the back is against a wall. Choose four-sided coverage when the table may be viewed from behind or when hidden storage is important. For a runner, plan where staff will stand and where brochures or products will sit so the logo remains visible.
Match the style to the venue
Indoor conferences often allow more control over the setup. Outdoor markets add wind, rain, damp ground, and uneven surfaces to the planning process. A branded[ custom pop-up tent](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/custom-pop-up-tents) can provide overhead shelter, but the tent, table, and any display accessories still need appropriate anchoring and safe placement.
For a round or cocktail-height table, use a cover made for that shape rather than forcing a rectangular cloth into place. For a portable check-in or sampling station, a complete table-and-cover kit may be more practical than sourcing each component separately.
Consider packing and repeat use
The best style is one your team can install, remove, clean, fold, and store consistently. A loose throw may be quick to position. A fitted cover may require more attention to corners and zippers. A stretch cover needs careful handling so the fabric is not caught on sharp hardware. A runner is easy to swap when campaigns change, but it still needs a clean, dry storage method.
Design and Branding Advice
Keep the front panel simple
Visitors usually see the front first. Put the logo, organization name, or short descriptor in a location that remains visible when the table is loaded. Keep important text away from seams, corners, zippers, and areas that fold over the edge.
One strong logo and one concise message are usually more useful than a paragraph of copy. If the cover will support lead generation, use a short call to action only when it can be read quickly from several feet away.
Design for the whole format
A throw, fitted cover, and stretch cover may expose the front, sides, and sometimes the back. Check how the artwork wraps around corners. A runner has a narrower visual area, so reserve clear space for the central logo and avoid placing critical information near the ends.
Use the artwork template for the exact style and size. Product pages may list accepted file types and preferred formats, but the correct template is the best way to check panel orientation, bleed, and safe areas.
Coordinate the table with the rest of the booth
A cover should support the booth rather than compete with it. Pair a strong table graphic with a restrained backdrop, or use a simpler cover when the back wall already carries a large campaign message. For a larger fabric system, review[ portable 8-foot display options](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/trade-show-displays/8ft-displays) and[ tension fabric display options](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/trade-show-booths/tension-fabric-displays), then keep colour, logo scale, and message hierarchy consistent.
Outdoor brands may also coordinate the table with[ straight flags](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/straight-flags/) or a canopy. Repeat the logo and key colours, but do not duplicate every line of copy on every surface.
Venue and Setup Considerations
Before the event, confirm whether the venue supplies a 4-foot, 6-foot, 8-foot, round, or cocktail table. Ask about table height, depth, placement, power access, aisle clearance, and rules for stored materials. Some venues may request documentation for fire resistance or other material requirements. Verify the exact product documentation and the venue’s current rules rather than assuming that a general material description is sufficient.
At setup, put the cover on before placing heavy items on the tabletop. Smooth the front, check that corners are seated correctly, and keep the hem or runner away from walking paths. Store boxes under the table only when the venue permits it, and keep staff access clear.
For an outdoor setup, check the forecast and have a plan for wind and moisture. A waterproof or water-resistant fabric description does not make the whole display weatherproof. Protect printed fabric from sharp edges, allow damp material to dry fully, and store it clean and dry after the event.
If the table is part of a larger branded environment, a[ 10x10 event kit with a printed table cover](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/10x10-trade-show-kit-full-walls-printed-table-cover) can help coordinate the table with walls and other display elements. A[ 10x10 deluxe event booth kit](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/10x10-deluxe-event-booth-kit-walls-flag-table) offers another package format to compare, while a[ 10x15 package with a table cover](https://www.signagebuzz.ca/10x15-pop-up-logo-tent-table-cover) serves the same planning purpose for a larger footprint. Review what is included in any package before assuming that a table, cover, or carrying case is part of the order.
Best Uses for Each Style
•Throw: General trade shows, conferences, registration desks, school events, and vendor tables where flexibility matters.
•Fitted: Corporate booths, information counters, photographed displays, and settings where a tailored appearance is important.
•Stretch: Modern product demonstrations, technology events, premium promotions, and setups viewed from several angles.
•Runner: Retail counters, campaign refreshes, sponsor tables, and organizations that already own a plain base cover.
A style can work in more than one setting. The best match comes from the combination of table shape, staff workflow, visitor movement, branding goals, and venue rules.
Custom Tablecloth Checklist
Before ordering, confirm the following:
•Measure the exact length, depth, height, and shape of the table.
•Confirm whether the table is rectangular, round, or cocktail height.
•Choose a throw, fitted, stretch, or runner format.
•Decide between three-sided and four-sided coverage where offered.
•Confirm rear access needs and under-table storage plans.
•Check the product’s material, care instructions, and intended use.
•Review venue rules for fire documentation, table coverage, and aisle clearance.
•Use the artwork template for the exact size and construction.
•Keep key text away from seams, corners, zippers, and folded edges.
•Approve the proof for spelling, colours, orientation, and panel placement.
•Plan how the cover will be packed, transported, cleaned, dried, and stored.
•Bring a setup plan for outdoor wind, rain, uneven ground, or changing conditions.
Frequently Asked Questions
1. What is the difference between a throw and a fitted tablecloth?
A throw drapes loosely over the table, while a fitted cover is shaped more closely to the table dimensions. A throw offers more flexibility; a fitted cover creates a more tailored silhouette.
2. Is a stretch tablecloth the same as a fitted tablecloth?
No. Both can look close to the table, but a stretch cover relies on tensioned fabric, while a fitted cover uses a sewn shape designed for the table. Confirm the construction and fit requirements for the specific product.
3. Which tablecloth style is best for trade shows?
It depends on the table and the desired look. A throw is versatile, a fitted cover looks structured, a stretch cover looks modern, and a runner works when a plain base already exists.
4. Should I choose a three-sided or four-sided cover?
Choose three-sided coverage when staff need rear access or seating space. Choose four-sided coverage when you want fuller concealment and branding around the table.
5. Can I use a runner without a full tablecloth?
You can, but the result depends on the table surface and venue expectations. A runner is usually intended to add branding over a plain tablecloth or another suitable base.
6. What table sizes are commonly available?
The cited SignageBuzz rectangular pages organize options around 4-foot, 6-foot, and 8-foot tables. Always confirm the exact finished dimensions and product configuration before ordering.
7. How do I measure for a fitted or stretch cover?
Measure the actual table length, depth, height, tabletop thickness, corners, and leg placement. Share unusual features with the supplier before selecting a close-fitting cover.
8. Can a rectangular cover be used on a round table?
It is not recommended for a polished result. The hem will not follow the table shape evenly. Select a cover designed for the table’s shape.
9. Where should the logo go on a tablecloth?
Place the primary logo on the front panel where it will remain visible above products and literature. Check side panels as well if visitors will approach from multiple directions.
10. How much text should go on a custom table cover?
Keep it brief. A logo, organization name, short descriptor, or concise call to action is usually easier to read than a paragraph, especially in a busy event aisle.
11. Can I use the same artwork on a throw, fitted cover, and stretch cover?
You may be able to reuse the brand elements, but the layout should be adapted to each construction. Seams, corners, zippers, and tension can change how artwork appears.
12. Are custom tablecloths suitable for outdoor events?
Some products describe water-resistant or waterproof and UV-related features, but outdoor suitability varies by product and conditions. Confirm the exact construction and secure the entire setup for wind.
13. What should I do if the venue supplies the table?
Ask for the table’s exact dimensions and shape in advance. If the venue cannot confirm them, a more flexible throw or a runner may be easier to plan than a fitted or stretch cover.
14. How should I store a printed tablecloth?
Remove debris, follow the product’s care instructions, and let the fabric dry completely before folding. Keep it away from sharp or abrasive hardware during transport and storage.
15. Can a table runner support a seasonal campaign?
Yes. A runner can make it easier to change the message while keeping a neutral base cover in service. Check that the new runner fits the table and leaves the artwork visible.
16. Should the back of the table be covered?
Cover the back when the table can be viewed from behind or when you want to conceal stored items. Leave it open when staff access, seating, or quick storage retrieval is more important.
17. Does the tablecloth include the table?
Not necessarily. Many cover and runner listings are for the printed fabric only. Read the package contents carefully, especially when comparing a cover with a complete table-and-cover kit.
18. What should I check before approving the proof?
Check spelling, logo proportions, colours, panel orientation, seams, corners, zipper areas, and the relationship between the artwork and the selected table size. Confirm that the proof matches the product configuration you intend to buy.
Conclusion
Throw, fitted, stretch, and runner covers each solve a different event-display problem. Choose a throw for flexible, traditional coverage; a fitted cover for a crisp tailored profile; a stretch cover for a sleek tensioned look; or a runner for focused branding over an existing tablecloth. Start with the actual table, decide how staff will use the space, and design the visible panels for quick reading. With the right fit and a clear proof, your table can become a practical, consistent part of the entire branded setup.
